points.description: Lower bound argument: with k queries, each index i gets a membership vector in {0,1}^k (which queries include it). Valid reasoning that these vectors must be nonzero (an index never queried cannot be determined) and pairwise distinct (if two indices are in exactly the same queries, their values cannot be separated, e.g. swapping/distinguishing x_i, x_j is impossible), so 2^k − 1 ≥ 2021, giving k ≥ 11. Equivalent valid arguments earn the mark.
points.partial_credit: Half credit if only distinctness or only non-zero is argued, or the bound 2^k ≥ 2021 is used without justification.

points.description: Upper bound construction: with 11 queries, assign each index a distinct nonzero 11-bit vector (2^11 − 1 = 2047 ≥ 2021) and query by bit position; shows that the answers let Bob recover every x_i (e.g., using pairwise coprimality, x_i = gcd of the products of queries containing i divided out appropriately, or gcd of query answers containing i with coprimality to separate indices by differing bits).
points.partial_credit: Half credit if the construction is stated but the recovery of each x_i is not justified.

points.description: Final answer stated as 11, with all steps valid (any wrong step means no credit for the whole solution per the grading rule).

rubric.notes: Full marks need the correct answer 11, with both a valid lower bound (distinct nonzero subset-vectors, 2^k−1 ≥ 2021) and a valid construction. Part marks for one half of the argument. Wrong final answer or invalid steps earn nothing.
rubric.answer_key: Answer: 11. Each index needs a distinct nonzero membership vector over the k queries, so 2^k − 1 ≥ 2021 forces k ≥ 11. Conversely, 2^11 − 1 = 2047 ≥ 2021, so assign distinct nonzero 11-bit codes and query by bit; for each prime p dividing some answers, the set of queries p appears in identifies the unique index (code) containing p, recovering every x_i.
